Future Flight Global Agrees to Buy Up to 20 Alia All-Electric Aircraft from Beta
7 photos
Photo: Future Flight Global/Instagram
The latest deal signed by Beta Technologies involves a reputable operator in the mobility management sector, and even the signing of the agreement was original and symbolic, marking the beginning of a new era where all-electric aircraft take center stage.
Signing an in-flight agreement for the purchase of several all-electric aircraft is symbolic in itself, and there was no better way to do it for two CEOs that are also both pilots. Karan Singh, founder and CEO of Future Flight Global, is a Boeing 737 airline captain with 5,000 hours under his belt, while Kyle Clark, founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, is a Beta test pilot and certified flight instructor, with more than 200 test flights in the Alia aircraft alone.
Beyond the strong symbolism of this signing up in the clouds, the agreement marks a serious commitment from FFG to purchase ten Alia aircraft, with the option for ten more units. The Alia CTOL, which is the conventional takeoff and landing version of the Alia all-electric aircraft, was at the center of this new purchase agreement.
Alia CTOL’s biggest selling point is that, unlike its eVTOL (vertical takeoff and landing) counterpart, it’s compatible with existing airport infrastructure and doesn’t require dedicated infrastructure. This makes CTOLs much easier and faster to deploy in regular commercial operations.
For now, we know that FFG intends to operate these all-electric aircraft for regional mobility service, but the cooperation with Beta is meant to expand further than that. FFG hinted at potential joint operations in international markets at some point, and it’s also working on a AAM (Advanced Air Mobility) multipurpose model for a wide range of applications, from passenger transportation and eco-tourism to medical missions, defense logistics, and cargo.
Beta’s Alia CTOL has already earned a solid reputation beyond US borders. This past summer, the UK-based Loganair has confirmed that it will become the first on the continent to operate a fleet of five all-electric aircraft, following a purchase agreement with Beta for five Alia aircraft, and the option of five more units.
Prior to that, in 2023, Alia was the first of its kind to be officially selected for Air New Zealand’s Mission Next Gen Aircraft Program, a large-scale initiative designed to find the best clean flight alternatives that could eventually replace Air New Zealand’s conventional fleet. Air New Zealand officially ordered one Alia CTOL, with the option for two more, and has recently conducted tests as part of an intensive Demonstrator program.
Back home, in the US, Beta has recently wrapped up its participation in the historic eIPP (eVTOL and electric aircraft Integration Pilot Program), and it was a blast. In Florida, the last state for Beta’s flight demonstrations, the Alia CTOL has completed 14 flights in the Orlando and Tampa regions, a total of almost 700 nautical miles.

This Is the Family Tree of the World’s Fastest Runway-Launched Jet Aircraft
20 photos
Photo: Hermeus
For a number of years now, an American aviation company called Hermeus has been occasionally making the headlines thanks to its work on something that would ultimately become not only the fastest runway-launched jet aircraft in history, but also the world's fastest operational aircraft of any kind, period.
Over these rather short years, the company has managed to reach several milestones, but, in doing so, it also created a bit of confusion, at least for outside eyes, regarding its products and plans. Luckily, earlier this month, Hermeus detailed each of the prototypes it has made and will make before the actual production jet is ready.
A sort of family tree, if you will, of an aircraft design that could change military aviation, and, if the Gods allow, the civilian one as well.
Quarterhorse Mk 0 The first test prototype the company has ever made, the Quarterhorse Mk 0, ended its testing period in the final months of 2023. Although it was powered by a General Electric J-85 jet engine, it didn't actually fly, but did run up and down the runway several times over a period of 37 days.
The design was used by Hermeus engineers to determine what it would take, going forward, when it comes to manufacturing, integration, and test processes. It also provided the team working on the project with data on airframe design, engine control, and wireless communication.
Quarterhorse Mk 1 Photo: Hermeus Building on that, Hermeus created the next iteration of the Quarterhorse , the Mk 1. It, too, powered by a General Electric J-85 jet engine and imagined in a delta wing configuration, took to the sky over the Edwards Air Force Base in the spring of 2025.
The flight was not about performance and breaking records, but about informing Hermeus about things like ground and flight controls and their behavior during take-off, flight, and landing.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 The next iteration of the design, the Mk 2, switched engines, going for a Pratt & Whitney F100, and grew to be about the same size as an F-16, from which it borrowed some components, including the landing gear.
As the first of three planned aircraft from the Mk 2 iteration, this uncrewed plane managed to reach supersonic speeds in May 2026, more specifically Mach 1.21 (928 mph/1,494 kph). It then steadily increased speeds in subsequent flights, reaching Mach 1.6 (1,227 mph/1,975 kph). The design also flew with an undisclosed payload, previewing the way the production version will work.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.2 Photo: Hermeus Just two months ago from the time of writing, in September 2026, an improved Mk 2.2 Quarterhorse began testing using upgraded avionics, software, and the so-called Gryphon propulsion system.
Mentioned for the first time by Hermeus in an operational setting, the Gryphon is a precooler-turbine based on the Pratt & Whitney F100 engine. Comprising an actuated spike inlet and the engine itself, it allows proper operation at a range of speeds that are inaccessible to regular turbines.
Hermeus presently uses this design to validate the propulsion architecture that would eventually take the aircraft past the Mach 2 (1,534 mph/2,469 kph) barrier.
Quarterhorse Mk 2.3 This upcoming version of the design is being imagined as a means to test thermal management of the jet, and it will be built using new concepts and materials. The focus of the testing program for this one will also include the collection of data on stability and control as it will approach Mach 3 (2,301 mph/3,704 kph), meaning ramjet speeds.
Quarterhorse Mk 3 and Mk 4 Photo: Hermeus This is when the company's F100–based Chimera ramjet technology, which until now has only been tested on the ground, will come into play in the air. This powertrain will operate in turbine mode at low speeds and in ramjet mode as soon as higher-Mach speeds are reached.
Hermeus says the Mk 3 will be built around an all-new high-temperature airframe, and that it will use the Chimera II turbine-based combined-cycle (TBCC) propulsion system. This will make it, for all intents and purposes, the first aircraft to use such a design, and, if everything works according to plan, the fastest runway-launched jet in history.
The Mk 4, using the lessons learned with the Mk 3, will try to maintain ramjet speeds for longer at higher altitudes, setting the stage for the world's fastest operational aircraft, the ultimate goal of this project, to come into play. For now, this uncrewed drone, if you will, is referred to as the Darkhorse .
It's unclear when the production versions will be ready, but when it gets here, it will be capable of hitting Mach 5 (3,800 mph/6,100 kph). This will make it a very valuable tool for the needs of the American defense industry, but, sadly, it seems plans for a civilian version are no longer in play, at least not in the foreseeable future.
When it first made the headlines, Hermeus talked about something called the Halcyon, a commercial aircraft capable of carrying a small number of passengers at insane speeds, fast enough to cover the distance from London to New York, for instance, in just one and a half hours. As a reminder, it takes present-day aircraft some eight hours to do this today.

Father-Son Project Must Go, 1957 Chevy Bel Air Already in Primer, Still a Big Restoration
45 photos
Photo: eBay seller menjiva66
Say what you want about a 1957 Bel Air , but such a car deserves a complete restoration, regardless of its condition. This specimen is living proof, as the father-son project must go to someone else with enough time to finish the work.
While we don’t know much about this car and its past, it looks like most of the work was aimed at the metal part. The Bel Air is now dressed in primer, though this doesn’t mean that everything outside is already in perfect shape.
“The passenger door opens but does not open all the way,” the seller explains. “The tie rod on the driver’s side is not installed correctly,” they continue.
So yes, this is a car that still requires extensive work, and the photos revealing the cabin are the living proof.
Photo: eBay seller menjiva66 The 1957 Bel Air was the model that marked the end of the Tri-Five decade, and it did the whole thing in a way that earned the car a place in history books. It paved the way for more V8 power, with Chevrolet getting serious about offering more muscle under the hood of its cars.
The 1957 Bel Air got a new V8 engine that eventually powered most cars in Chevrolet’s lineup. The 265 was bored out to 283 cubic inches, and the resulting Turbo-Fire became an iconic configuration that continued to be refined throughout the rest of the decade.
It was just the beginning of the V8 party, with a 348 big-block engine seeing daylight a year later with the debut of the Impala and a 409ci configuration going live early in the next decade.
The 283 joined the Bel Air lineup in multiple configurations, beginning with a two-barrel setup that used a single exhaust and produced 185 horsepower.
Customers who wanted more power in their Bel Air (or 210, as Chevrolet offered the same engine options across nearly the entire lineup) could get the Super Turbo-Fire, which replaced the two-barrel with a four-barrel and benefited from a higher compression ratio. The result was impressive, as the power rose to 220 horsepower.
Corvette configurations in the Bel Air lineup increased the power output to a maximum of 270 horsepower, but the top choice was the fuel-injected setup with 283 horsepower when solid lifters were installed. Ramjet engines are rare and troublesome, but they still make for great - and very, very expensive - collectibles, especially if they benefit from an all-original and unmolested Bel Air to show what they’re capable of.
Photo: eBay seller menjiva66 This Bel Air that’s still in the works comes with a 302/350 combo, but that’s all the information we know about the engine and the transmission.
Based on the photos shared by the seller on eBay, the engine might be in good shape, but that’s just an assumption, and I would still recommend that you call them for additional information before you ask your mechanic to inspect everything live.
The vehicle requires extensive work in the cabin, where this ongoing restoration probably has stopped. The interior is a sign that this Bel Air had probably been sitting for quite some time before it ended up in the hands of this restoration guy, though the photographs suggest that the vehicle has somehow remained complete.
This is fantastic news for a car this old, as not serving as a donor for another project allows for an easier restoration, especially if sticking as close to the original specimen as possible is a priority.
Photo: eBay seller menjiva66 Otherwise, I do believe that this Bel Air is worth a chance. Many of these cars end up getting a 350 under the hood, most often paired with aftermarket upgrades, such as custom interiors, modern audio systems, and shiny new paint. There’s no reason this won’t happen on this Bel Air, assuming that the right restoration guy comes across this specimen.
I still believe that pricing makes a huge difference, especially because this Bel Air has already embraced a direction. The owner looks confident they would be able to get $20,000 on the car, and I think that this expectation is realistic if the car comes with a running engine and most of the mechanicals already in good shape.
If the cabin requires most of the work, this Bel Air is a great project for someone who just wants to give the finishing touches to a 1957 car. Otherwise, getting that much for this car might be quite challenging, so call the seller, ask all these questions, and then you can turn to the Make Offer button on eBay to submit your offer.
The vehicle is parked in Palmdale, California, and you will need transportation to move it from its current garage to your restoration shop to complete the job. The listing ends in 21 days, so you have three full weeks to get all the information you need to make an informed decision towards a potential purchase.

1995 Acura NSX-T Had Just One Owner For a Quarter of Century, Has Less Than 57k Miles on Odometer
9 photos
Photo: Garage Kept Motors / Instagram
Sitting proudly in the inventory of Grand Rapids, Michigan-based Garage Kept Motors , this crimson 1995 Acura NSX-T has the 'T' standing for Targa, of course, and rocks the Formula Red exterior hue on a classic, pristine black leather interior.
The description is pretty straightforward: the Honda/Acura NSX was “conceived as a car to show the Italians how to make a supercar without compromises; the NSX is a complete masterpiece of thoughtful engineering with the first all-aluminum chassis and body in the automotive world, useful ergonomics, legendary reliability, a design with some Pininfarina blood, and tactile handling massaged by the man himself: Ayrton Senna.” Yep, that nicely sums up what the Japanese intended back in the early 1990s.
A few model years later, the 1995 Acura NSX-T was already a landmark in Japanese sports car engineering, combining the European-style and pretty exotic mid-engine performance with the precision and everyday usability that made Honda and Acura models true legends for their customers, the NSX included. Well, here’s an excerpt of that, dressed with a cool Targa body to let you enjoy a scenic drive with the wind in your hair.
Finished in Formula Red over a black interior, this 1995 Acura NSX-T has just 56,668 miles on the odometer and, more importantly, a track record of being for 26 years in the care of the same owner. “Power comes from a naturally aspirated 3.0-liter V6 mounted behind the passenger compartment,” of course, and it’s also equipped “with the four-speed automatic, representing the grand tourer side of the line, that can be shifted via a small lever just behind the steering wheel, making this an early ‘Tiptronic’ setup allowing you to make the C30A sing while enjoying the talkative steering and responsive suspension.”
As a reminder, the Acura NSX came with lightweight aluminum construction, a sophisticated independent suspension, and a mid-engine layout that provided great balance and handling, “while its power-assisted steering and carefully engineered chassis make it approachable for everyday driving.” The original helped establish new benchmarks for exotic sports cars, and the “NSX-T designation identifies this car as a targa-roof model, featuring removable roof panels that allow drivers to enjoy open-air motoring while retaining the distinctive proportions of the NSX coupe.”
The Formula Red finish contrasts beautifully with the well-taken-care-of black interior, featuring “supportive seating, clear instrumentation, and thoughtfully arranged controls with the visibility and comfort that distinguish it from many contemporary exotic cars.” Of course, this example isn’t selling cheap: the dealership wants no less than $119,900 to part ways with it, putting it right in the path of a contemporary mid-engine sports car – the C8 Chevrolet Corvette.
So, it’s either this NSX or a brand-new 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport X , which kicks off at $110k sans destination and rocks the all-new 6.7-liter V8 engine from the Stingray and Grand Sport alongside the ZR1X electrification components, giving it a combined total of no less than 721 horsepower. So, what do you think – yay or nay?

The 2027 Alliance Valor 4310 Debuts as a Fifth-Wheel Toy Hauler That Really Feels Like Home
20 photos
Photo: YouTube/Markhams on the Move
Utility doesn't exclude comfort or aesthetics, though that often seems to be the case with utility-focused fifth-wheel toy haulers. This one wants to be the exception, and while still in prototype stage, you can't but admit that it makes a compelling argument.
This is the Alliance Valor 4310, which is being presented as a 2027 model year but is in reality still just a prototype. It's a fully functional one, though, and it's actually being put through its paces by the couple posting RV content under the Markhams on the Move handle.
The rig was not developed with or built for the Markhams, though they did take delivery of it after Alliance debuted at a recent dealer event, where it was brought out to gauge potential interest in it. As you must know, many big RV companies got in on the deal with rising RV content creators, designing one-off custom units in a sort of partnership agreement, with the view of launching a production floorplan if there was enough interest in that custom unit.
This isn't one of them, but similarities exist. The Markhams say that they already owned a 2023 Alliance that they were looking to upgrade and that they'd been looking specifically into the new Valor 4213 floorplan. They toured that one but did not love it, so they asked for the 4310, of which they'd heard on the grapevine.
Photo: YouTube/The RV Hunter The moment they saw it, they knew it was "the one." At the time they shot the first video below, they'd lived in it for one week and had it set up, but were yet to travel in it, which they planned to do soon. The rig will serve as their permanent home, and the first thing they loved about it was how residential it felt.
It seems that this residential quality was the main focus from the start, as Hunter from The RV Hunter also points out. The Valor 4310 is a fifth-wheel toy hauler that feels like an actual home, where most toy haulers feel like toy haulers with a house attached.
This being a prototype, exact dimensions are still pending, but you're looking at a big and heavy rig , sat on a 101-inch (256-cm) widebody chassis and a triple axle with H-rated Continental tires and upgraded MORryde CRE3000 suspension. It will come standard with an upgraded Curt Helux pinbox, six-point hydraulic auto-leveling, three exterior awnings, and three flush-floor slide-outs, one of which is a super-slide.
Photo: YouTube/The RV Hunter You're also looking at a nice toy hauler with a 14-foot (4.2-meter) garage with a rear patio, complete with a Thule awning, safety railing and gate, and all the necessary tie-downs for your gear. At the same time, though, this garage brings extra functionality, whether you need a mobile office space, an extra bedroom with sleeping for as many as five or six people, or additional storage.
Unlike other garages onboard toy haulers, this one comes with a full dry bathroom, which means that the extra functionality as a bedroom isn't just an afterthought, as well as insulated floors, TV and entertainment, and a separate entrance.
Then, there's the "livability" of the rest of the space . Thanks to the widebody chassis and the smart design, the rest of the rig is a proper home, complete with an island kitchen with a standalone dinette, a generously sized living room with a massive sectional that is equal parts chillout-perfect and a spare bed for two, and a king bedroom with a walk-in wardrobe, heaps of storage, and a pass-through bathroom.
Photo: YouTube/The RV Hunter Styling is residential, too. This toy hauler offers solid surface counters, residential appliances, and solid wood furniture, as well as prep for an optional washer and dryer (in the bedroom space) and all the storage space an entire family might need, regardless of how much time they plan to be spending on the road.
The little comforts of residential life are included. You get a coffee hutch with subway tile backsplash off the kitchen, an island with a massive, all-accessory stainless steel sink, a dedicated pantry with sensor lights, and plenty of space to move around. You get a dinette that will be as comfortable for game nights as it will be for hosting dinner parties.
Features highlighted by Alliance and/or obvious in the video tour below include atrium tinted windows in the living room space and the dinette, extra tall slide-outs, JBL two-zone audio, a TV on a televator in the living room so you can still enjoy the view when you're not tuning in on your favorite movies and shows, Furrion Chill Cube ACs, and a sectional sofa in the living with everything from accent lighting to hidden cup holders and reclining functions.
Photo: YouTube/The RV Hunter Also standard is a full-time RV-ing warranty, Tufflex roof with a telescopic ladder for access, a molded front cap, separate compartments for lithium batteries and a backup generator, a dedicated metal box for tools and other items, and an auxiliary fuel tank for the garage – assuming you will want to actually haul toys in this rig.
As of this writing, the Alliance Valor 4310 is in prototype phase, but the floorplan will debut as a standalone luxury fifth wheel floorplan for the 2027 model year. When that happens, the full list of specs will be made public, but don't let its absence stop you from taking it it visually.
Via // The RV Hunter on YouTube

About the author: Elena Gorgan
Elena has been writing for a living since 2006 and, as a journalist, she has put her double major in English and Spanish to good use. She covers automotive and mobility topics like cars and bicycles, and she always knows the shows worth watching on Netflix and friends. Full profile

If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.
Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.
Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.
It’s the humble 125cc motorcycle.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The world’s default vehicle isn’t a car
Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.
But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.
The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.
They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.
You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.
And I’ve done it myself to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.
Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.
My time (briefly) testing a borrowed 125cc motorbike in the Philippines
Electric should be perfect here
The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.
These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.
A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.
Unlike replacing a heavy-duty pickup truck that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.
Royal Enfield’s Flying Flea C6 is one of the few examples of a light electric motorcycle designed for this role
Yet the West largely skipped this category
Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.
We have electric bicycles , and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to premium electric motorcycles costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.
Thankfully, that seems to be changing.
The ONYX RCR became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.
Ryvid’s Anthem pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.
The new LiveWire S4 Honcho also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.
Even Infinite Machine’s Olto , while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.
These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.
Infinite Machine’s Olto is a lightweight, easy-to-ride electric scooter that can carry two riders anywhere in a city
Maybe we’re obsessing over the wrong EV
Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.
But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.
Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.
A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.
We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.
Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.
A Ryvid Anthem e-motorcycle could replace most car trips in the US, and the ‘fuel’ is so cheap that it’s almost free
Most trips don’t require two tons of metal
Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.
Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home. Occasionally , there’s another passenger.
Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.
I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.
Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.
Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.
My wife and I traveled everywhere we wanted to go in Menorca on a 110cc Honda
They don’t need to replace every car
This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.
No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.
Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.
But it doesn’t have to.
If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.
Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.
Motorcycles work fine in the rain, and millions do it every day. The question is whether you work in the rain.
The infrastructure problem almost disappears
One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.
DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.
The simplicity is almost refreshing.
And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like Gogoro in Taiwan or Vammo in South America that can make charging unnecessary.
Infinite Machine’s Olto battery even charges at home in a convenient little dock
They’re approachable
Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.
That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.
Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.
The LiveWire S4 Honcho brings 125cc-equivalent electric motorcycles to the masses for an affordable $4,999 – and even has reverse!
Europe already understands the category
One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.
Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.
Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.
North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.
The Yamaha XENTER E electric scooter brings 125cc-equivalent performance to Europe
A new generation is already telling us what it wants
Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.
The explosion in popularity of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.
Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.
Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should recognize it as an opportunity . Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.
If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.
Teens today are riding small off-road electric dirt bikes, but those same riders could be tomorrow’s commuters
Maybe we’ve been looking in the wrong direction
One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.
I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.
But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.
Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.
Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

Just Update Your Car Already: Police Issue New Warning for Kia and Hyundai Owners
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Screenshot from YouTube video
This is becoming utterly frustrating for pretty much everybody, including the police, but Kia and Hyundai owners are once again prompted to update their cars. The alert comes from police in the city of Sheboygan, Wisconsin, which is just one of the many regions where the Kia Boys are still doing their thing almost four years after the whole thing started.
Police in the city say that the number of thefts and attempted thefts specifically aimed at Kia and Hyundai cars is growing again. The easiest way to make sure your car is not stolen is to install the anti-theft update that dealerships are offering for free.
The Kia Challenge started in 2022 when a video published on TikTok highlighted a vulnerability in certain Kia and Hyundai models manufactured between 2011 and 2021. The video rapidly went viral, essentially putting a crosshair on the back of every Kia and Hyundai car parked outside.
The whole thing went out of control, and this is how the Kia Challenge started. Teens, who make for an important part of the TikTok audience, founded the infamous Kia Boys group, leading to thousands of cars being stolen for joyrides and Internet fame.
Kia and Hyundai responded fast with a software update that prevents the engine from being started using the method described on social media. The Kia Boys typically break into these cars by smashing the glass or messing with the door handle. Once inside, they remove the steering wheel column cover and need just a USB cable, typically left by the car owner inside the cabin, to start the engine.
Photo: WTHR on YouTube/Alissa Smart The software update blocks the engine from starting unless the original key is being used, as long as the car is locked with the key fob.
Unfortunately, not all Kia and Hyundai owners have installed the update. The patch is free of charge and can be deployed at any Kia and Hyundai dealer. The number of thefts still happening across the United States confirms that many cars are still exposed to the hack, therefore keeping the Kia Boys busy.
The Sheboygan police tell car owners to park in well-lit areas, as this is a way to keep the Kia Boys, who are typically trying to do their thing without being noticed, from smashing the side glass. Additionally, police officers recommend that car owners install steering wheel locks or other anti-theft devices to prevent the Kia Boys from driving away even if they get inside.
Kia and Hyundai are also giving away steering wheel locks to customers whose cars can’t be patched. If a vehicle isn’t eligible for the anti-theft patch, it can be further protected against the TikTok hack using a steering wheel lock or with an ignition cylinder protector that makes it harder for the Kia Boys to start the engine.
Photo: WTHR on YouTube/Alissa Smart Similar recommendations have previously been shared by police departments in many other regions throughout the United States. Officers at the Metro Nashville Police Department published a call for owners to patch their cars, explaining that without Kia and Hyundai owners actually installing the anti-theft update, stopping this viral trend is close to impossible.
“It’s a trend that’s lingered the last few years & we need YOUR help to make it harder on those committing crimes in our city,” the Metro Nashville Police Department explained in a post. “Call your local dealership or check if your car requires the FREE recall online.”
In addition to steering wheel locks, owners are also recommended to install trackers to help police officers determine the location of stolen cars and, therefore, assist them as they try to recover the vehicles and catch the Kia Boys. AirTags are particularly efficient in this case, and police in several regions gave away Apple trackers specifically for Kia and Hyundai owners who want to install an additional layer of protection in their cars.
Photo: WTHR on YouTube/Alissa Smart AirTags are pill-shaped devices that use CR2032 batteries to offer up to six months of battery life per unit. Thanks to Find My integration, AirTags communicate with the owner’s iPhone using nearby Apple devices. An AirTag doesn’t offer a built-in Internet connection and relies on Bluetooth to connect to nearby devices that are already online. The owner can just launch the Find My app on their iPhone, iPad, or Mac or check the web version of the platform to see the location of the AirTag, according to the latest update.
AirTags can be planted virtually anywhere in the car, and considering many Kia Boys use iPhones, as Apple’s smartphones are particularly popular among teens, there’s a good chance that the location data is updated frequently in the Find My app, even if it gets stolen.s
Kia and Hyundai have never published any statistics as to how many vehicles on the road are still vulnerable to the TikTok vulnerability. Owners can check whether their cars can be patched using the VIN checker published on Kia’s and Hyundai’s websites.

Novitec-Tuned Lamborghini Temerario Looks Like a Chic Gotham City Prop
20 photos
Photo: Instagram | novitecgroup
Do all exotic models with a black overall look seem like they could easily be a Gotham City prop? Well, most of them do, and even if that may sound like a cliché, it is what it is. And in this case, it is a tuned Lamborghini Temerario, as mentioned in the title.
Signed by Novitec and shared on social media not long ago, this machine easily stands out from the crowd, and proves that blue-blooded rides do not need lively paint finishes in order to make a statement, because a fully-black example can also do that. Well, an almost fully black one, because the brake calipers were actually painted purple in order to tie the supercar’s exterior to the cockpit.
That’s because this modded Lamborghini Temerario has quite a few purple touches on the inside, which can be seen on the seats, on the sides of the center console, some parts of the dashboard, and the door cards. White piping and contrast stitching can also be seen inside this machine. The dominating color is black, and it is a mix of leather and Alcantara upholstery that was wrapped around most touchable surfaces.
The top parts of the dashboard panel, the pillars, headliner, steering wheel, and other components were wrapped in Alcantara. The usual amount of carbon fiber trim is also on deck. The Raging Bull’s logo was embroidered into the integrated headrests, Lamborghini’s name adorns the dashboard in front of the passenger, the Temerario name greets users upon opening the doors, and the OEM emblem is still found on the steering wheel.
Photo: Instagram | novitecgroup Those who are unfamiliar with the design of the Lamborghini Temerario might be tempted to say that things such as the apron, the front hood, the side skirts, ducktail spoiler-like element at the rear, diffuser, and probably other parts on the outside have come from the aftermarket world. But they haven’t, because Novitec hasn’t signed them. These components are actually the OEM ones, just like the headlights, taillights, and so on.
The wheels, on the other hand, with their quite intricate design, are a novelty, and even if they may wear the Raging Bull’s corporate logo on the center caps, they are new. They’re called the NL7, and even if Novitec may not mention Vossen’s name in the social media post embedded at the bottom of the page, we know that these two companies have teamed up on countless projects over the years.
A set of sport springs, which seem to have brought the car’s body a bit closer to the asphalt, are also part of the makeover. And so is the exhaust system, which is said to give the V8 engine a “ more emotional soundtrack .” However, in order to retain the OEM appearance , Novitec decided to keep the original tailpipes. Thus, even if the exhaust system is indeed new, the tips aren’t.
And yes, it is a V8 engine that powers Lamborghini’s new “baby” supercar, in case you forgot, as while its predecessors, the Huracan and Gallardo, had naturally aspirated V10s, the Temerario uses a 4.0-liter mill with twin turbocharging. On top of that, the ICE is assisted by no fewer than three electric motors, because this model is a plug-in hybrid, just like Lambo’s entire modern-day lineup that also comprises the Revuelto and the Urus SE Performante.
Photo: Instagram | novitecgroup In total, the Lamborghini Temerario has 907 hp (920 ps/677 kW) to play with, with the ICE kicking out 789 hp (800 ps/588 kW) between 9,000 and 9,750 rpm. The supercar is 0.2 seconds slower than the Revuelto and 0.3 seconds slower than the new Revuelto SV, taking 2.7 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill. Keep the right pedal pinned to the floor where the road and legislation allow it, and you will eventually see mph (343 kph) on the digital speedometer behind the steering wheel.
This one of the three screens inside the Temerario, which starts at approximately $400,000 for the 2027 model year in the United States of America, alongside the portrait-oriented infotainment system, and the tiny display in front of the passenger.
We’ve said it before and we will say it again: Novitec can easily host a tuning course , regardless of the project, and most of its builds prove that less is indeed more in the tuning game. This particular Lamborghini Temerario stands out for all the right reasons, this writer believes, and it deserves its 15 minutes of online fame.
It is not the last Temerario that we will cover from this tuner, because the company is currently working on a fully exposed carbon fiber package, said to come later this year. And knowing how Novitec rolls, we can already tell that we will definitely dig that makeover, just like this one. But the question is, do you agree that the pictured Lambo is on the cool side of things? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Novitec Group (@novitecgroup)

Suzuki-Backed Japanese eVTOL Gears Up for Commercial Service in South Korea
8 photos
Photo: SkyDrive
SkyDrive has entered a tripartite agreement with Goyang Special City and Verty to establish a comprehensive framework that will eventually support regular commercial operations for the Japanese eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) in South Korea.
Earlier this week, during the DRONE-UAM EXPO 2026 event, held at KINTEX in Goyang, visitors had the opportunity to take a closer look at a small, 20-percent-scale mockup of the SD-05, SkyDrive’s flagship aircraft. The exhibition was co-hosted by SkyDrive and Verty, a Seoul-based company specializing in integrated systems and air traffic management solutions for vertiports.
Goyang Special City is set to become an AAM (Advanced Air Mobility) hub. It was officially designated the primary metropolitan demonstration site for South Korea’s famous national K-UM Grand Challenge, and it’s currently working on multiple levels to advance AAM operations, from building vertiport testbeds to training future aerospace workforce in collaboration with Korea Aerospace University.
Together, SkyDrive, Goyang Special City, and Verty will work to establish an ecosystem for upcoming flight trials and commercial eVTOL services in Goyang. If things fall into place, commercial operations could kick off as soon as 2028.
SkyDrive doesn’t just have an award-winning eVTOL design, but also the adequate large-scale manufacturing capabilities, thanks to its strong ties to Suzuki Motor Corporation. Two years ago, the Japanese company officially confirmed that it would begin aircraft production at a facility owned by Suzuki. In 2025, Suzuki also helped seal the deal between SkyDrive and the Gujarat-based JetSetGo Aviation Services for a huge pre-order of up to 50 SD-05 aircraft.
This week, Japan’s Finance Minister, Satsuki Katayama payed a special visit to SkyDrive, which included a short flight demonstration , as well as discussions of future manufacturing plans with Suzuki representatives.
Earlier this year, SkyDrive was granted the ADO (Approved Design organization) certification from JCAB (the Japan Civil Aviation Bureau), the equivalent of the ODA (Organization Designation Authorization) from FAA in the US. With that certification in hand, SkyDrive became the first AAM company in Japan to reach this far in the type certification process.
Like all eVTOL makers, SkyDrive is aiming for international success beyond the national borders of Japan. Right now, it’s cooperating on commercialization projects with operators and authorities in ten countries.
This also includes the US. This past summer, SkyDrive kicked off official meetings with FAA representatives for the type certification procedures in the US. Back in 2023, the Japanese company had set up a local subsidiary here, specifically to facilitate its official entry on the American market. In 2024, SkyDrive’s type certificate application, submitted through JCAB, was officially accepted by the FAA.
SkyDrive’s SD-05 was purposely designed as a compact passenger eVTOL and an alternative to the heavier eVTOLs on the market. It targets short-distance urban flights of around 15 km (9 miles) at a top speed of 100 kph (62 mph).

Cavorite X7 to Become a Medical Aircraft for Northern Ontario Indigenous Communities
8 photos
Photo: Horizon Aircraft
While eVTOLs (electric vertical takeoff and landing) were originally developed with urban air mobility in mind, hybrid-electric VTOLs have immense potential for improving access to and from remote locations and communities, thanks to their extended range. The Canadian-made Cavorite X7 has exactly what it takes to provide lifesaving air services to Indigenous communities.
Constance Lake First Nation (CLFN) is an Oji-Cree and Cree community, whose members live on the shores of Constance Lake, close to Hearst in Northern Ontario. Despite the beauty and natural richness of the region, limited access to emergency medical transportation is one of the major setbacks. The geographical location and the harsh weather conditions make it difficult for critical patient transfer and deliveries to operate as they should.
A new agreement between CLFN and Horizon Aircraft is about to change that for the better. Based on this MoU, the Cavorite X7 could operate as a lifesaving medical aircraft for the community, although an official number of aircraft wasn’t yet specified.
The Cavorite X7 has what it takes to fulfill this difficult role. First, it has the speed and range to access these remote areas faster than conventional medevac helicopters, with no need for a dedicated runway.
Another important aspect that makes it better than conventional helicopters is the certified ability to operate in conditions of low visibility, snow, and extreme cold. This means it will be able to ensure critical air service year-round, in a region where bad weather is frequent and where such services are currently non-existent.
Although CLFN was the first to sign an official agreement to start operating Cavorite X7 aircraft, other Indigenous communities could eventually benefit from this as well. In fact, Horizon Aircraft Co-Founder and CEO Brandon Robinson believes that this Canadian-made, hybrid-electric VTOL could become “a national model” for better critical air mobility in remote communities.
One of the first hybrid-electric VTOLs ever made, the Cavorite X7 sports Sci-Fi-looking transforming wings that reveal 12 lift fans during the vertical takeoff, and then conceal them during the forward flight phase (that’s when they’re covered by sliding panels). This innovative fan-in-wing design improves speed, range, and harsh weather operations, compared to standard helicopters on one side, and open-rotor eVTOLs, on the other side.
The seven-seat configuration is another feature that sets apart the Cavorite X7. This was an upgrade from the original design, the Cavorite X5. Coupled with a range of up to 800 km/500 miles (mid-load, with fuel reserve) at a 450 kph/250 knots cruise speed, this configuration makes the Cavorite X7 one of the best options out there for regional air mobility.
The Canadian-made hybrid-electric VTOL is currently targeting Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) and Flight Into Known Icing (FIKI) certification, in partnership with the Flight Centre of Excellence and the University of Toronto.

Dealer Uncovers 1957 Ford Thunderbird That Spent Decades in a Heated Garage, Not All Good News
42 photos
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay
Locked in heated storage. That’s pretty much all you need to know about this Ford Thunderbird if you’re trying to figure out its condition. The car looks great, considering it doesn’t boast a recent restoration, and the only urgent work it needs is under the hood.
The dealer responsible for finding a new home for this T-Bird says it loud and clear: this car needs to be gone through to get to safe, running condition.
A full restoration doesn’t seem to be required, considering the overall shape, but asking your mechanic to open the hood and inspect everything in there is obviously recommended.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay The battle for the number one spot in the American car space was getting fiercer in 1957. With Chevrolet launching a new Bel Air, whose new major selling point was the 283 Turbo-Fire, Ford also needed to focus more on engine power. This is why an upgraded version of a 312 ended up seeing the rollout in 1957. The supercharged engine produced no more, no less than 300 horsepower.
The base Thunderbird continued to be offered with a 292, while the 312 was offered as an option with three power configurations, namely 245, 270, and 285 horsepower. In terms of transmissions, Thunderbird buyers could choose between 3-speed manuals, overdrives, and the famous Ford-O-Matic automatic.
Ford’s strategy worked, as the company secured the leading spot for another year before losing it in 1958 when the Impala came out. Ford ended the year with 21,380 T-Birds rolling off the assembly lines, with 1957, therefore, becoming the most successful year of this nameplate until that point.
The Thunderbird was slated to get bigger changes in the following years, with a larger model planned for 1958. However, the battle in this space was getting fiercer, especially as General Motors started focusing more on full-size cars with a completely redesigned lineup planned for the 1958 model year .
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay This particular Thunderbird is fitted with a 292 engine paired with a Ford-O-Matic transmission. We’re not getting any insights into this engine’s past, but it’s safe to assume that this is the original configuration.
As the dealer explains, the engine turns over but does not currently run. However, considering it’s been sitting in a heated garage, bringing it back to life should be totally doable, especially considering that the engine was running prior to being parked.
I would still ask my mechanic to go there in person and check the engine in person, as retaining the original engine, even if it’s the base setup, should be a priority for every buyer.
Still fitted with the removable factory hardtop, this Thunderbird looks to be in good shape, and you can tell it’s been stored in the right conditions. The non-running engine is probably a victim of the car not being regularly started, but otherwise, the rust clearly hasn’t taken its toll on this Thunderbird.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay If you’re particularly interested in the mileage, this is where things get tricky. While the car has been parked for 20 years, so you’d normally expect it to be a low-mile specimen, the true mileage is actually unknown.
The odometer shows 13,122 miles, which would be a fantastic number for a 1957 car, but the actual mileage isn’t known at this point.
It’s difficult how original and complete the car continues to be after all these years, but the seller reveals that the T-Bird needs new tires, but comes with an original-style dashboard.
Photo: Imports & Classics on eBay This Thunderbird is undoubtedly an intriguing presence, especially thanks to its condition. But without answers to the big questions, including regarding the previous ownership and the work this car has already received, it’s hard to think that it would just sell overnight.
An in-person inspection and more details offered by the dealer are must-haves, so contact them with all your questions if you’re interested in a purchase.
Otherwise, just be ready to pay $26,000 for this car. The dealer believes this is a fair price, but the Make Offer option has also been enabled, so with the right negotiation skills, you might be able to get a better deal. I wouldn’t expect the price to drop significantly though, so maybe $25,000 is the best deal you could get.
Meanwhile, the vehicle is parked in Bellingham, Washington, and considering the engine is no longer running, you should also find transportation. This could be a problem for someone living far from this location, as the final cost of the acquisition would increase significantly.
The listing is set to expire in 7 days, so theoretically, you have enough time to convince your significant other, call the dealer, get all the information you need, and then go there in person to see the Thunderbird with your own eyes. Make sure you also ask about the documentation that could be available with this car, including the build sheet.
